title: How NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX Unlocks Ultrafast Interactivity at Long Context on NVIDIA Vera Rubin | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA reports the first third-party benchmark of Groq 3 LPX — Artificial Analysis measured 3,431 output tokens/second on Gemma 4 31B at 100K context, and 3,382 at 10K, showing near context-length-independent speed — and positions the deterministic, compiler-scheduled LPU rack as the high-interactivity tier of the Vera Rubin platform. The mechanism is minimizing first-bit latency via preplanned chip-to-chip transfers across 256 LP30 LPUs with 128 GB of SRAM and 96 links per chip at 112 Gbps, with three named co-execution modes pairing LPX racks to Vera Rubin NVL72 for models projected up to 2 trillion parameters.

themes.theme: Long context as the agentic constraint

insights.claim: Multiturn agentic sessions append each turn's output to a continually growing context, so context reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens once sessions exceed hundreds of turns and the agent must reprocess everything it has learned late in a task.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Token consumption per task grows superlinearly with session length — the demand driver behind inference capacity forecasts, and the reason KV-cache capacity is becoming a purchasing spec.
insights.locator: Why is long context at high interactivity important?

insights.claim: Model quality alone does not determine agent capability — limited context caps agentic capability regardless of how fast or smart the underlying model is.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Reframes competition from model benchmarks toward serving-system context capacity — a point of differentiation that favors hardware vendors over model labs.
insights.quote: No matter how fast or smart the underlying model, limited context means limited agentic capability.
insights.locator: Without long context, agents can only take into account

insights.claim: Interchip transfer time decomposes into first-bit latency (link selection, endpoint synchronization, conflict arbitration) plus transfer time (data volume over bandwidth), and at small batch sizes the fixed first-bit component dominates because the data being moved is tiny relative to available bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: The cleanest mental model for why bandwidth spec sheets mislead on interactive inference — latency, not bandwidth, is the binding constraint at the high-interactivity end of the Pareto.
insights.locator: the amount of total time each individual transfer takes has two components

insights.claim: Tensor parallelism can deliver order-of-magnitude speedups but requires very small batch sizes for the highest interactivity, and at those batch sizes fixed coordination cost can exceed the time saved by distributing the computation.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Explains why throughput-optimized GPU racks cannot simply be dialed down to serve latency-critical traffic — it is an architectural split, justifying a separate accelerator tier.
insights.quote: But the highest levels of interactivity require very small batch sizes, where the fixed coordination cost can outweigh the time saved from TP.
insights.locator: Why is serving models at ultrafast interactivity with long context challenging?

insights.claim: A Groq 3 LPX rack exposes 256 LP30 local processing units to the compiler, which has full visibility into individual compute units and produces a down-to-the-clock-cycle schedule of the entire workload before it begins.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Determinism is the architectural bet: it eliminates runtime arbitration but makes the compiler the single point of failure and the hardest asset for competitors to replicate.

insights.claim: The rack carries 128 GB of total SRAM-based memory collectively across the 256 chips and 96 chip-to-chip links per chip running at 112 Gbps each, with each LPU able to act as a router as well as a processor.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: 128 GB of SRAM across a whole rack is a hard capacity ceiling — it explains why LPX is paired with Vera Rubin NVL72 for large models rather than serving them alone, and why the KV cache must live elsewhere in some configurations.
insights.quote: The 96 C2C links per chip running at 112 Gbps each
insights.locator: Groq 3 LPX uses a deterministic execution model.

insights.claim: Precomputed scheduling removes the request/confirm/contend handshake that normal systems perform per transfer — LPUs send data on the clock cycle it is ready and consume it on the clock cycle it arrives.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: The elimination of real-time arbitration is the specific source of the latency advantage — worth testing whether it survives dynamic MoE routing and variable-length agentic traffic.

insights.claim: The LPX compiler schedules compute and communication at the granularity of 320-byte vectors, exploiting the fact that matrix multiplication is a series of dot products to begin sending output columns as soon as a 320-byte slice is ready rather than waiting for the full matrix operation.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: 320-byte granularity overlap is the mechanism that makes tensor parallelism pay at batch sizes where it normally does not — the technical claim competitors must match.
insights.quote: the compiler schedules workloads on its compute and communication units at the level of 320-byte vectors

insights.claim: Artificial Analysis measured a median 3,431 output tokens/second on Gemma 4, a 31B-parameter dense model released in April 2026, at 100K input context — presented as the first third-party benchmark of Groq 3 LPX performance.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Third-party validation is the credibility unlock for a new accelerator tier; but note it is a 31B dense model, not a frontier MoE, so the result does not yet generalize to production frontier serving.
insights.quote: Artificial Analysis has run its 100K context benchmark on the Gemma 4 31B model on Groq 3 LPX, measuring a world-class interactivity of 3,431 output tokens/second.
insights.locator: In this post, we report the first third-party benchmark

insights.claim: The benchmarked system was stood up by NVIDIA in its own data centers rather than a customer or neutral facility, a vendor-controlled configuration caveat on the headline number.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Treat these figures as best-case demonstrations until an independent cloud provider publishes comparable numbers on production traffic.
insights.quote: An NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX system NVIDIA has stood up in its own data centers generated answers at 3,431 output tokens per second (Figure 7).
insights.locator: Groq 3 LPX achieves leading interactivity at 100K context

insights.claim: At 10K context the same system delivered a median 3,382 output tokens/second versus 3,431 at 100K — under 2% variation — meaning the deterministic architecture makes serving speed largely independent of context length.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Flat speed versus context is the genuinely differentiated property here — GPU serving typically degrades with context, so this is the claim to verify against competing stacks.
insights.quote: they found that Groq 3 LPX answered at a median speed of 3,382 output tokens per second
insights.locator: Artificial Analysis also benchmarked the same system at 10K context length

insights.claim: On the open-source SPEED-Bench coding benchmark with the same Gemma 4 model, Groq 3 LPX produced a median 4,767 output tokens/second and a P80 of 5,520, meaning over 20% of problems generated faster than 5,500 tokens/second.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Coding-specific throughput exceeding the general benchmark suggests output-shape sensitivity; useful for anyone modeling cost-per-completed-coding-task rather than cost-per-token.
insights.quote: the NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX system produced answers to these coding questions at a median speed of 4,767 output tokens per second and a P80 of 5,520 output tokens per second

insights.claim: NVIDIA states today's most popular agentic tools run closer to 60 tokens per second, against which decoding 5,000 tokens takes about 1.5 seconds on LPX versus 50 seconds at 100 tokens/second — a 30x-plus experiential gap.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: A concrete baseline for the current market: if incumbent agentic tools serve at ~60 tok/s, there is a large latent upgrade cycle in inference infrastructure for anyone selling interactivity.
insights.quote: Even this comparison is generous, since today’s most popular agentic tools run closer to 60 tokens per second.
insights.locator: At this rate, decoding 5,000 tokens takes about 1.5 seconds

insights.claim: Artificial Analysis and NVIDIA both confirmed the benchmarked configuration had no loss of precision or model quality in its outputs, pre-empting the usual objection that speed records come from aggressive quantization.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Quality-neutrality is the diligence question on every speed claim; its explicit inclusion signals NVIDIA expects that attack.
insights.quote: Testing by Artificial Analysis and NVIDIA confirmed that the NVIDIA configuration for both of these benchmarks had no loss of precision or model quality in its outputs.
insights.locator: Testing by Artificial Analysis and NVIDIA confirmed

themes.theme: LPX plus Vera Rubin co-execution roadmap

insights.claim: Groq LPU technology is now marketed as a first-party NVIDIA product line — 'NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX' positioned as the interactive inference accelerator for the Vera Rubin platform, with an NVIDIA VP of LPU Compilers among the authors.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: NVIDIA absorbing the leading low-latency inference challenger removes the most credible non-GPU alternative for interactive serving and consolidates the inference accelerator landscape.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX is the interactive AI inference accelerator for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX is the interactive AI inference accelerator

insights.claim: Three named co-execution configurations pair the two rack types: standard prefill-decode disaggregation with Vera Rubin handing off KV cache once per turn; attention-FFN disaggregation where Vera Rubin holds KV in DRAM and LPX runs FFN layers; and external-drafter speculative decoding with LPX running the draft model.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous rack pairing means AI factory buildouts need two accelerator types plus a high-bandwidth inter-rack link — a more complex and more NVIDIA-dependent capex plan.
insights.quote: Only intermediate tokens are sent between racks, once per full-attention layer.
insights.locator: Pairing this new low latency, deterministic execution capability

insights.claim: NVIDIA projects a scaled-up GPT-OSS model at 2 trillion parameters running across Vera Rubin NVL72 plus Groq 3 LPX — a projection, not a measurement, of multi-trillion-parameter high-interactivity serving.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Separate the measured 31B dense result from the projected 2T claim — the gap between them is where the real engineering and commercial risk sits.
insights.quote: Figure 11 shows a projection of a scaled-up GPT-OSS model to 2 trillion parameters running on Vera Rubin NVL72 and Groq 3 LPX.
insights.locator: All of these enable each rack to focus

insights.claim: NVIDIA expects rack-wide low-latency SRAM access to sustain the measured speed into the multi-hundred thousands of tokens of context, an expectation rather than a benchmarked result.
insights.speaker: Seth Weidman
insights.so_what: Context-length headroom beyond 100K is the next benchmark to demand; the 128 GB rack SRAM budget is the obvious constraint to test it against.
insights.quote: With low-latency access to SRAM across the rack, we expect to be able to maintain this speed into the multi-hundred thousands of tokens.
insights.locator: With low-latency access to SRAM across the rack
